item.title: The Witcher 3 Is a Great Story Trapped Inside an Overrated RPG
item.description:
Sometimes, it seems like it's difficult to have a discussion about the greatest RPGs of all time without someone bringing up The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt . And of course, there's usually that one person who's ready to challenge this claim by pointing out the game's awkward mechanics and rather underwhelming combat. In any case, there seems to be one thing that most people can agree on, and that's just how good the game's story actually is. The writing, and therefore its narrative, has everything players could wish for, which has certainly earned its reputation as one of the most well-written titles out there.

However, being great at storytelling doesn’t automatically mean that the mechanics are just as good. And this is important, because once a player experiences the repetitive combat and clumsy character progression, they might start reconsidering whether the game's overall reputation is entirely justified. And although CD Projekt Red has already proven with Cyberpunk 2077 that they can create a much more engaging RPG experience, maybe it's time to question whether The Witcher 3 is actually a better story than it is a game.

The Witcher 3 Remastered and Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Seem to Have Their Labels Backward

The Witcher 3 Remastered and Ocarina of Time Remake are taking surprisingly opposite approaches to what should change and what should stay.

By Josh Cotts

The Witcher 3's Repetitive Combat Makes Monster Preparation Feel Pointless

One of the biggest issues with The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt has always been its combat system, and most people seem to agree that its repetitiveness can get old pretty quickly. Yes, Geralt has access to both silver and steel swords, and he can use magical Signs, dodge attacks, and even throw the occasional bomb, but even with all of these tools, many fights can be handled by just using the same old combination of sword attacks and dodging. In a game like The Witcher 3 , this could easily be deemed unforgivable simply because the game has a great foundation for making its encounters way more interesting.

For example, the Bestiary provides information about different creatures, while the oils and potions are great for pre-battle prep. So, the concept of preparation is there, but once you reach the battle, you quickly find out that there really wasn’t much to prepare for in the first place, which many people label as a huge waste of opportunity. At least with a story as great as the one we have here, one could always turn a blind eye to these shortcomings and focus on the story instead, which it seems like many players are already doing anyway.

Cyberpunk 2077 Shows What The Witcher 3's RPG Progression Is Missing

Unfortunately for The Witcher 3 's defenders, maybe combat is not the only area where their favorite game struggles to compete with Cyberpunk 2077 . When it comes to character progression, Geralt certainly has plenty of abilities to unlock, but the sad truth is that there's only so much players can do with him. Yes, they can invest in Combat, Signs, and Alchemy, but in general, Geralt will always be just Geralt, regardless of how you distribute the points. And although this doesn't seem like much of an issue when a game is built around an established protagonist, it definitely limits to what extent players can change their approach. In an RPG, most people would expect a lot more freedom when it comes to character builds and how their choices affect character progression.

Cyberpunk 2077 's Update 2.0 introduced a major overhaul of the game's perk trees and cyberware systems in September 2023.

On the other hand, we have Cyberpunk 2077 , where players can specialize in everything from stealth to melee combat and firearms, which creates characters with genuinely different strengths. Especially after Update 2.0, the game's progression system became even more flexible, shifting toward perks that unlock more substantial abilities. Moreover, cyberware adds yet another layer of customization by allowing players to install technological enhancements that improve their abilities even further. In other words, while The Witcher 3 revolves solely around making Geralt better at what he already does, Cyberpunk 2077 gives players considerably more freedom to decide what type of character they want to be.

Maybe The Witcher 3's Brilliant Storytelling Overshadows Its RPG Shortcomings

Of course, none of this criticism changes the fact that The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt has exceptional writing. Geralt's decisions have insane consequences that extend far beyond the regular conversation quest and even affect other characters. This is certainly impressive, especially considering that the decisions players are presented with are usually quite complicated as well. However, there's a difference between being one of the greatest written games ever made and being one of the best RPGs of all time.

The Witcher 3 Is a Great Story Trapped Inside an Overrated RPG
The Witcher: 5 Open-World RPGs That Surpassed Wild Hunt, Officially Ranked
The Witcher 3's Gwent Designer Just Revealed a Crueler Card Game
The Witcher 3 Remastered Mods Prove Why Skyrim Still Matters

Cyberpunk 2077 is a great example of what CD Projekt Red is actually capable of delivering when it comes to combat and character progression, and maybe this distinction proves that The Witcher 3 's shortcomings could actually have been avoided. In any case, it would be interesting to see whether The Witcher 3 would still be held in such high regard if it wasn't for the exceptional writing. But one thing cannot be denied—very few games have stories so compelling that players are ready to overlook just about everything else.

9 /10

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt

Getting a few extra resources can make it easier to get your garden going. The available codes offer Cash, Mango Seeds, and Luck Potions, along with other free rewards to help you along the way. item.title: Enshrouded's 1.0 Release Is Putting Steam's Early Access Promise on Trial
item.description:
Whether players like it or not, it’s now clear that Steam Early Access has become a pretty convenient arrangement for some developers. It is just oh so marvelous to release an unfinished game but still charge people while continuing to work on it without having to commit to a release date. Steam's Early Access program was designed specifically to allow devs to work on their projects while involving the players in the process. This is not an inherently evil idea, and Enshrouded is a good example of why, but when the development process seems to have no end in sight, the situation can become quite sticky.

Thankfully, Enshrouded is one of the games that will remind people what Early Access is supposed to look like. It entered the program on January 24, 2024, and is now scheduled to reach version 1.0 on October 15, 2026 . Sure, that's almost three years of development, but this is nothing unusual when it comes to game development. Moreover, the fact that Keen Games has committed to a specific release date already sets it apart from games that seem perfectly content to remain in Early Access indefinitely.

New Steam Feature Is a Game-Changer for Early Access Games

Steam launches a new feature that is a potential game-changer for early access titles, and likely to be welcomed by developers and players alike.

1
By Dominik Bošnjak

Enshrouded Is Showing What an Early Access Commitment Should Look Like

It's no secret that when Enshrouded first entered the Early Access program, Keen Games had some pretty ambitious plans. The studio wanted to add new biomes to the world, introduce more enemies, and even give players more crafting materials and equipment. Of course, these are all very important in a survival RPG, especially one that is in its early stages of development, but the studio also made it clear that it wanted the players to have a say in what happens. More specifically, people were strongly encouraged to share their opinions on Discord, Steam Forums, and the in-game feedback system.

This means that Keen Games actually used the game's Early Access stage as an opportunity to deliver a better title at the end, instead of simply charging people indefinitely. Then, on June 25, 2026, the studio announced the release date for version 1.0, and here we are. It's rare to see a game developer commit to a concrete release date, especially when remaining in Early Access indefinitely is always an option. After all, we've all witnessed games like 7 Days to Die , which spent more than a decade in Early Access before finally reaching version 1.0.

A Release Date Alone Won't Make Enshrouded a Finished Game

Announcing a release date and sticking to it is cool and all, but players are all too well aware that this is only half of the job. After all, there's not much point in removing the Early Access tag if the game still feels unfinished. Thankfully, it seems like Keen Games is fully aware of this fact. In August 2026, the studio discussed its ongoing preparations for version 1.0, including work on existing mechanics and systems.

Enshrouded 's full release is planned for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S.

And although some people might prefer to get an overwhelming amount of new content instead, polishing what is already there may turn out to be equally important; if the game doesn't run properly in the first place, then there's almost no point in adding anything else. Ultimately, it seems like Keen Games is aiming to deliver a well-balanced 1.0 version, so it's safe to say that the game's biggest challenge might be making sure that everything feels polished enough to justify taking the game out of its Early Access phase.

Enshrouded Could Remind Developers What Early Access Is Actually For

It's true that Enshrouded is just one game in a world where thousands of games are released every year, and maybe one title isn't enough to make a significant change. However, it has certainly raised some interesting questions regarding the relationship between developers and players. According to Steam's guidelines, Early Access is not supposed to be used simply as a way to fund development, and there's no guarantee that these games will ever be finished at all. But just because players have been warned about the risks doesn't mean that developers are free from responsibility.

Enshrouded's 1.0 Release Is Putting Steam's Early Access Promise on Trial
Games With Deep Base-Building Freedom
PS5 Getting 16-Player Open World Co-Op Survival Game
Best Rogue Daggers Build in Enshrouded (2026)

The thing is, trust goes both ways. Of course, Enshrouded will probably not change the industry, but its upcoming full release could encourage other developers to take their own Early Access commitments more seriously. Even more importantly, this could change the way players approach Early Access as well and make them more willing to give smaller studios a chance. And considering how brutal the industry is to independent developers, this would most certainly be a welcome change.

Whether players like it or not, it’s now clear that Steam Early Access has become a pretty convenient arrangement for some developers. It is just oh so marvelous to release an unfinished game but still charge people while continuing to work on it without having to commit to a release date. Steam's Early Access program was designed specifically to allow devs to work on their projects while involving the players in the process. This is not an inherently evil idea, and Enshrouded is a good example of why, but when the development process seems to have no end in sight, the situation can become quite sticky.

Thankfully, Enshrouded is one of the games that will remind people what Early Access is supposed to look like. It entered the program on January 24, 2024, and is now scheduled to reach version 1.0 on October 15, 2026 . Sure, that's almost three years of development, but this is nothing unusual when it comes to game development. Moreover, the fact that Keen Games has committed to a specific release date already sets it apart from games that seem perfectly content to remain in Early Access indefinitely.

New Steam Feature Is a Game-Changer for Early Access Games

Steam launches a new feature that is a potential game-changer for early access titles, and likely to be welcomed by developers and players alike.

1
By Dominik Bošnjak

Enshrouded Is Showing What an Early Access Commitment Should Look Like

It's no secret that when Enshrouded first entered the Early Access program, Keen Games had some pretty ambitious plans. The studio wanted to add new biomes to the world, introduce more enemies, and even give players more crafting materials and equipment. Of course, these are all very important in a survival RPG, especially one that is in its early stages of development, but the studio also made it clear that it wanted the players to have a say in what happens. More specifically, people were strongly encouraged to share their opinions on Discord, Steam Forums, and the in-game feedback system.

This means that Keen Games actually used the game's Early Access stage as an opportunity to deliver a better title at the end, instead of simply charging people indefinitely. Then, on June 25, 2026, the studio announced the release date for version 1.0, and here we are. It's rare to see a game developer commit to a concrete release date, especially when remaining in Early Access indefinitely is always an option. After all, we've all witnessed games like 7 Days to Die , which spent more than a decade in Early Access before finally reaching version 1.0.

A Release Date Alone Won't Make Enshrouded a Finished Game

Announcing a release date and sticking to it is cool and all, but players are all too well aware that this is only half of the job. After all, there's not much point in removing the Early Access tag if the game still feels unfinished. Thankfully, it seems like Keen Games is fully aware of this fact. In August 2026, the studio discussed its ongoing preparations for version 1.0, including work on existing mechanics and systems.

Enshrouded 's full release is planned for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S.

And although some people might prefer to get an overwhelming amount of new content instead, polishing what is already there may turn out to be equally important; if the game doesn't run properly in the first place, then there's almost no point in adding anything else. Ultimately, it seems like Keen Games is aiming to deliver a well-balanced 1.0 version, so it's safe to say that the game's biggest challenge might be making sure that everything feels polished enough to justify taking the game out of its Early Access phase.

Enshrouded Could Remind Developers What Early Access Is Actually For

It's true that Enshrouded is just one game in a world where thousands of games are released every year, and maybe one title isn't enough to make a significant change. However, it has certainly raised some interesting questions regarding the relationship between developers and players. According to Steam's guidelines, Early Access is not supposed to be used simply as a way to fund development, and there's no guarantee that these games will ever be finished at all. But just because players have been warned about the risks doesn't mean that developers are free from responsibility.

Enshrouded's 1.0 Release Is Putting Steam's Early Access Promise on Trial

The thing is, trust goes both ways. Of course, Enshrouded will probably not change the industry, but its upcoming full release could encourage other developers to take their own Early Access commitments more seriously. Even more importantly, this could change the way players approach Early Access as well and make them more willing to give smaller studios a chance. And considering how brutal the industry is to independent developers, this would most certainly be a welcome change.

item.title: No Man's Sky Announces Brand-New Release for October 28
item.description:
No Man's Sky is officially getting a new release on October 28, bringing the universe-exploring game to even more people. No Man's Sky has come a very long way since its original launch, and now it's passing another major milestone.

No Man's Sky originally launched a decade ago, and is one of the most successful instances of a game arriving as a disappointment, only to turn it around in a big way. Over the years, updates have added new content and gameplay mechanics, turning No Man's Sky into a major hit that still sees tens of thousands of players daily on Steam alone.

No Man's Sky Players Have Explored Less Than 1% of Its Planets, But Starfield Is Too Big

No Man's Sky is 10 years old now, and the game has continued to tackle space exploration in a way that Starfield has struggled to.

By LB Beistad

No Man's Sky Gets New Release

No Man's Sky will officially launch for iPhone and iPad devices on October 28. The game isn't a "lite" mobile version, but rather a full experience, with over forty of the major updates the existing versions of the game have received over the years, including the recent Cosmos update. Impressively, the game only demands 4GB worth of storage, and the team at Hello Games has worked hard to make it compatible with a significant number of iOS devices. The game can be played on iPhone 11 and up, and 3rd generation iPad Air and above, with the App Store confirming the game will require iOS 26 or later, and a device with the A12 Bionic chip or better. Players can check out the beginning of the game for free, with the full title costing $19.99.

However, there are some missing features and other factors to consider with the mobile iOS version of the game. No Man's Sky 's Planetary Settlements feature will only be available to users on iPhone 15 Pro or better, and the game will completely lack multiplayer at launch. While the team hasn't directly promised to eventually add said feature, it did point out that the Switch version launched in a similar state, and eventually grew to include more on the Switch 2 version. If the iOS version performs well, the team will "support it appropriately," perhaps leading to additional features later on.

On the other hand, unique considerations and features went into bringing the game to iPhones and iPads. This version of No Man's Sky features touch-screen controls, but will provide support for controllers on all devices, plus mouse and keyboard for iPad, and players can cast the game to their TVs. The game has seen a "ton of work" put into maximizing battery life and reducing heat output, so that the game can be enjoyed for longer periods of time comfortably.

New Open-World Simulation Game on Steam Launches to 80% Very Positive Reviews
No Man's Sky Announces Brand-New Release for October 28

You Can Now Play BioShock in Co-Op

No Man's Sky is likely to see new players and more attention following the release of both the Cosmos update and this new iOS version. But Hello Games is already gearing up for what's ahead. Hello Games' next game, Light No Fire , will give players a multiplayer fantasy world survival sandbox to explore, survive, and develop together. The game seems like it's inspired by and includes much of the DNA and concepts that No Man's Sky has created and refined since its release, albeit on a single planet. While it currently lacks a release window, players can wishlist the game now.
